$$ \displaystyle\max\{\|{x_{\mathcal{T}}-{x}_{0}}\|,\|{y_{\mathcal{T}}-{x}_{0}}\|\} \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{ub}}}}\|z_{\mathcal{T}}\|\geq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{ub}}}}(\|p_{\mathcal{T}}\|-\|q_{\mathcal{T}}\|)\geq\frac{1}{4\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{ub}}}}\|p_{\mathcal{T}}\| \displaystyle\geq\frac{(1+\alpha\gamma)^{\mathcal{T}}\alpha\omega}{4\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{ub}}}}\overset{(a)}{\geq}\frac{2^{\iota/2-3}p_{\mathrm{lb}}}{\sqrt{p_{\mathrm{ub}}}\ell_{1}}\bar{\omega}\overset{(b)}{>}\mathcal{S}. $$

where in $(a)$ , we used the inequality $(1+x)^{1/x}\geq 2$ for every $0<x\leq 1$ and in $(b)$ , we used the definition of $\bar{\omega}$ . The above inequality contradicts with (56) and therefore completes our proof. ∎

### D.2 Proof of Lemma 29

To prove Lemma 29, first we provide an upper bound on $f(X_{t})$ .

#### Lemma 38.

For every iteration $X_{t}$ of PPrecGD, we have

$$ f(X_{t})\leq f(X_{0})+2\sqrt{\|X_{0}\|_{F}^{2}+\eta}\cdot\alpha\beta\epsilon $$

#### Proof.

Note that $f(X_{t+1})\leq f(X_{t})$ , except for when $X_{t}$ is perturbed with a random perturbation. Moreover, we have already shown that, each perturbation followed by $\mathcal{T}$ iterations of PMGD strictly reduces the objective function. Therefore, $f(X)$ takes its maximum value when it is perturbed at the initial point. This can only happen if $X_{0}$ is close to a strict saddle point, i.e.,

$$ \|\nabla f(X_{0})\|_{X_{0},\eta}^{*}\leq\epsilon,\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla^{2}f(X_{0})\not\succeq-\sqrt{L_{d}\epsilon}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{X_{0},\eta}, $$

Therefore, we have $X_{1}=X_{0}+\alpha\zeta$ , where $\zeta\sim\mathbb{B}(\beta)$ . This implies that

$$ \displaystyle f(X_{1})-f(X_{0}) \displaystyle\leq\alpha\langle\nabla f(X_{0}),\zeta\rangle+\frac{\alpha^{2}L_{1}}{2}\|\zeta\|_{F}^{2}\leq\alpha\left\|\mathbf{P}_{X_{0},\eta}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}\left\|\nabla f(X_{0})\right\|^{*}_{X_{0},\eta}\left\|\zeta\right\|_{F}+\frac{\alpha^{2}L_{1}}{2}\|\zeta\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}\sqrt{\left\|X_{0}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\eta}\cdot\epsilon\alpha\beta+\frac{L_{1}}{2}\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}\overset{(b)}{\leq}2\sqrt{\left\|X_{0}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\eta}\cdot\epsilon\alpha\beta $$

where $(a)$ follows from our assumption $\|\nabla f(X_{0})\|_{X_{0},\eta}^{*}\leq\epsilon$ , and $(b)$ is due to our choice of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ . This implies that $f(X_{t})\leq f(X_{1})\leq f(X_{0})+2\sqrt{\left\|X_{0}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\eta}\cdot\epsilon\alpha\beta$ , thereby completing the proof. ∎

The above lemma combined with the coercivity of $\phi$ implies that

$$ X_{t}\in\mathcal{M}\left(\phi(X_{0}X_{0}^{T})+2\sqrt{\|X_{0}\|_{F}^{2}+\eta}\cdot\alpha\beta\epsilon\right) $$

for every iteration $X_{t}$ of PPrecGD. Now, we proceed with the proof of Lemma 29.

#### Lemma 29.

First, we prove the gradient lipschitzness of $f(X)$ . Due to the definition of $\Gamma_{F}$ and Lemma 38, every iteration of PPrecGD belongs to the ball $\{M:\|M\|_{F}\leq\Gamma_{F}\}$ . For every $X,Y\in\{M:\|M\|_{F}\leq\Gamma_{F}\}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\nabla f(X)-\nabla f(Y)\right\|_{F} \displaystyle=2\left\|\nabla\phi(XX^{\top})X-\nabla\phi(YY^{\top})Y\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq\left\|\nabla\phi(XX^{\top})-\nabla\phi(YY^{\top})\right\|_{F}\left\|X\right\|_{F}+2\left\|\phi(YY^{\top})\right\|_{F}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 2L_{1}\Gamma_{F}\left\|XX^{\top}-YY^{\top}\right\|_{F}+5L_{1}\Gamma_{F}^{2}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 2L_{1}\Gamma_{F}\left\|X(X-Y)^{\top}-(Y-X)Y^{\top}\right\|_{F}+5L_{1}\Gamma_{F}^{2}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq 9L_{1}\Gamma_{F}^{2}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F} $$

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle\nabla^{2}f(X)[V],V\rangle-\langle\nabla^{2}f(Y)[V],V\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\left|\left\langle\nabla\phi(XX^{\top})-\nabla\phi(YY^{\top}),VV^{\top}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle+\left|\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(XX^{\top}),XV^{\top}+VX^{\top}\right\rangle-\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top}),YV^{\top}+VY^{\top}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 2\left\|\nabla\phi(XX^{\top})-\nabla\phi(YY^{\top})\right\|_{F} \displaystyle+\left|\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(XX^{\top}),XV^{\top}+VX^{\top}\right\rangle-\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top}),XV^{\top}+VX^{\top}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle+\left|\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top}),YV^{\top}+VY^{\top}\right\rangle-\left\langle\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top}),XV^{\top}+VX^{\top}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 2L_{1}\left\|XX^{\top}-YY^{\top}\right\|_{F} \displaystyle+\left\|\nabla^{2}\phi(XX^{\top})-\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top})\right\|\left\|XV^{\top}+VX^{\top}\right\|_{F} \displaystyle+\left\|\nabla^{2}\phi(YY^{\top})\right\|\left\|(Y-X)V^{\top}+V(Y-X)^{\top}\right\|_{F} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 4L_{1}\Gamma_{F}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F}+4L_{2}\Gamma_{F}^{2}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F}+2L_{1}\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F} \displaystyle= \displaystyle((4\Gamma_{F}+2)L_{1}+4\Gamma_{F}^{2}L_{2})\left\|X-Y\right\|_{F}. $$

Therefore, $f(X)$ is $((4\Gamma_{F}+2)L_{1}+4\Gamma_{F}^{2}L_{2})$ -Hessian Lipschitz within the ball $\{M:\|M\|_{F}\leq\Gamma_{F}\}$ . Finally, it is easy to verify that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{P}_{X,\eta}=(X^{T}X+\eta I_{n})\otimes I_{r}$ are between $\eta$ and $\Gamma_{2}^{2}+\eta$ within the ball $\{M:\left\|M\right\|\leq\Gamma_{2}\}$ . Moreover, $\left\|\mathbf{P}_{X,\eta}-\mathbf{P}_{Y,\eta}\right\|\leq\left\|X^{\top}X-Y^{\top}Y\right\|\leq 2\Gamma_{2}\left\|X-Y\right\|$ . This completes the proof of this lemma. ∎

# EPC PRE-EXECUTION PLANNING COMMUNICATION: A COMPARATIVE

# ANALYSIS OF FOUR APPROACHES

Gerardus Blesto1, Richardus N. Kasih2, Budi Utomo3, & Gregory F. Saragih4

# ABSTRACT

Communication during the pre-execution planning phase—encompassing scope definition, schedule development, and procurement strategy before field execution—is critical to the performance of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) projects, a delivery model in which a single contracting entity assumes integrated responsibility for engineering, procurement, and construction. Conventional EPC pre-execution planning communication is document-centric and contract-driven, providing traceability but limiting timely crossfunctional alignment and learning. Three alternative approaches—Lean Construction, Project Production Management (PPM), and Advanced Work Packaging (AWP)—propose distinct mechanisms to improve planning-phase communication. This paper presents a structured comparative analysis of these four approaches using criteria derived from EPC planning challenges, project communication literature, and socio-technical systems theory. The analysis shows that Lean Construction strengthens collaborative commitment, trust, and feedback loops; PPM introduces system-level flow logic and quantitative variability control; and AWP embeds communication within structured work packages aligned to construction needs. While each approach addresses specific limitations, none is sufficient in isolation. The findings are synthesized into an integrated communication architecture positioning Lean, PPM, and AWP as complementary across social, systemic, and procedural dimensions. This study contributes an analytical baseline, a comparison framework, and an integration model to support future research and implementation in EPC projects.

## KEYWORDS

Collaboration, commitment, trust, EPC projects, pre-execution planning.

## INTRODUCTION

Engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) projects are a project delivery model in which a single contracting entity assumes integrated responsibility for engineering design, procurement, and physical construction. This model is prevalent in sectors such as oil and gas, power generation, petrochemicals, and heavy industrial infrastructure, and is typically characterized by large scale, high technical complexity, and long supply chains. Within this context, effective communication is widely recognized as a critical determinant of project

Despite advances in digital tools and formal communication management systems, EPC projects continue to experience persistent coordination failures, rework, and misalignment traceable to deficiencies in early planning communication (Merrow, 2011; Flyvbjerg, 2014).

The pre-execution planning phase plays a particularly influential role (Kabirifar & Mojtahedi, 2019), encompassing scope definition, schedule development, procurement strategy, constructability review, and work breakdown structuring. During this phase, activities across engineering, procurement, and construction are both sequential and concurrent, yet decisions are taken under high uncertainty while locking in a significant proportion of project cost and risk (Miller & Lessard, 2000). This paper focuses on inter-organizational communication across these functional interfaces, as cross-functional coordination represents a distinctive and persistent source of planning failures in EPC projects (Shen et al., 2017; O'Connor et al., 2017).

Conventional communication practices in EPC pre-execution planning are predominantly document-centric and contract-driven, relying on formal deliverables, hierarchical reporting, and approval structures. While this provides traceability and contractual control, it results in fragmented information flows, delayed feedback, and limited cross-functional learning (Love et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2017). In response, three alternative approaches have emerged: Lean Construction, emphasizing collaborative planning and commitment-based coordination (Ballard & Howell, 2003; Koskela, 2000); PPM, focusing on flow, variability, and capacity through system-level planning logic (Hopp & Spearman, 2011; Rooke et al., 2012); and AWP, structuring planning communication through standardized work packages with explicit readiness criteria (CII, 2015; O’Brien et al., 2013 ).

Although increasingly applied in practice, these approaches are often presented independently and without clear comparison to conventional EPC communication. This paper addresses that gap through a structured, criteria-based comparison and integrative framework positioning them as complementary rather than competing, focusing on inter-organizational pre-execution planning communication across engineering, procurement, and construction. This advances Lean Construction discourse by situating collaborative practices within a broader socio-technical framing connecting them to production system logic and structured execution planning (Howell et al., 2011; Rooke et al., 2012).

## BACKGROUND AND THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS

COMMUNICATION IN EPC PRE-EXECUTION PLANNING

Communication in projects is commonly defined as the process through which information, meaning, and intent are created, transmitted, and interpreted among project stakeholders to achieve project objectives (PMI, 2021). In EPC projects, communication extends beyond simple information exchange and becomes a critical inter-organizational coordination mechanism across engineering, procurement, and construction functions that are tightly coupled in time but often organizationally separated.

EPC delivery structures concentrate contractual responsibility within a single entity, yet execution typically involves multiple internal departments, subcontractors, vendors, and external stakeholders. This configuration creates numerous organizational interfaces and increases communication complexity, particularly during early project phases when scope, design maturity, and execution strategies are still evolving (Shen et al., 2017; O'Connor et al., 2017). Prior studies have shown that ineffective communication across these interfaces is a major contributor to scope changes, rework, claims, and schedule delays (Love et al., 2016; Flyvbjerg, 2014). The pre-execution planning phase is especially sensitive because engineering decisions influence procurement lead times and construction sequences, while procurement constraints and constructability considerations must simultaneously inform engineering

DOCUMENT-CENTRIC COMMUNICATION IN EPC PRE-EXECUTION PLANNING

Conventional document-centric communication in EPC pre-execution planning is shaped by contractual requirements, quality management systems, and risk management considerations (Kabirifar & Mojtahedi, 2019). Communication is formal, hierarchical, and document-based, relying on drawings, specifications, schedules, transmittals, RFIs, and meeting minutes designed to ensure traceability and contractual compliance across organizational boundaries (PMI, 2021). While such systems provide necessary governance, information flows tend to be linear and sequential, feedback loops slow and reactive, and communication focused on transmission rather than shared understanding or collaborative problem-solving (Love et al., 2018). These characteristics reinforce functional silos and discourage early cross-functional integration (O'Connor et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2017).

LEAN CONSTRUCTION AND COLLABORATIVE PLANNING COMMUNICATION

Lean Construction emerged from production theory applied to construction, emphasizing the Transformation-Flow-Value (TFV) framework and the management of workflow and variability (Koskela, 2000). Communication is viewed as a social process enabling coordination, commitment, and learning—closely aligned with relational coordination theory, which emphasizes that high-frequency, timely, problem-solving communication embedded in relationships of shared goals and mutual respect is central to interdependent work performance (Gittell, 2002). In the pre-execution planning phase, practices such as pull planning and phase planning, as part of the Last Planner System (LPS), create structured forums for stakeholders to jointly define sequences, identify constraints, and make reliable commitments (Ballard & Howell, 2003). Research has shown that such practices improve planning reliability and crossfunctional alignment (Howell et al., 2011; Ballard et al., 2009). Lean communication also promotes trust and psychological safety—conditions identified as prerequisites for effective cross-functional collaboration (Edmondson, 1999)—though Lean approaches tend to provide limited formal guidance on integrating with production system design and EPC contractual controls.

PPM AND SYSTEM-LEVEL PLANNING COMMUNICATION

PPM applies operations science principles to project-based production, conceptualizing project execution as a network of interdependent activities whose performance depends on flow management rather than local task optimization (Hopp & Spearman, 2011; PPI, 2017). While PPM draws on manufacturing systems theory, its application to EPC contexts requires adapting these principles to conditions of high variability, unique deliverables, and evolving scope. Planning-phase communication is structured around defining system capacity, sequencing logic, buffers, and release conditions—communicating production rules and performance metrics rather than fixed schedules (Rooke et al., 2012). This reframes communication from a managerial coordination problem to a system design problem, providing a quantitative foundation for aligning engineering, procurement, and construction decisions. However, PPM operates primarily at an abstract system level and offers limited guidance on the behavioral and relational dimensions of planning communication.

AWP AND EXECUTION ORIENTED PLANNING COMMUNICATION

AWP was developed within the industrial construction sector to address misalignment between engineering, procurement, and construction. AWP structures planning communication by decomposing project scope into standardized work packages—Engineering Work Packages (EWPs), Construction Work Packages (CWPs), and Installation Work Packages (IWPs)—

In the pre-execution planning phase, AWP embeds communication requirements within work package definitions, specifying deliverables, interfaces, readiness criteria, and handoff milestones (O’Brien et al., 2013). Empirical studies indicate that AWP can improve schedule predictability, labor productivity, and planning reliability in EPC projects (CII, 2015; O'Connor et al., 2017). Nevertheless, AWP can become overly rigid or document-heavy without attention to collaborative behaviors and system-level flow logic, potentially reproducing limitations of conventional communication systems.

SOCIO-TECHNICAL SYSTEMS THEORY AS AN INTEGRATIVE LENS

Socio-technical systems (STS) theory, originating in the work of Trist (1981) and elaborated by Pasmore (1988), holds that organizations achieve high performance when their social subsystem—human relationships, norms, trust, and collaborative behaviors—is designed in concert with the technical subsystem—tools, processes, workflows, and information structures. Applied to EPC planning communication, STS theory provides a unifying perspective that connects Lean Construction's behavioral emphasis with PPM's technical system logic and AWP's procedural structures. This integrative framing is particularly relevant for the People, Culture and Change track, which recognizes that sustainable improvements in project production systems depend on cultural transformation, trust development, and behavioral change alongside technical redesign (Howell et al., 2011).

SYNTHESIS: IMPLICATIONS FOR COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

As demonstrated above, the four communication approaches embody fundamentally different assumptions. Document-centric systems prioritize governance and traceability; Lean emphasizes collaboration, trust, and commitment; PPM focuses on production flow and variability; and AWP operationalizes communication through structured work packages. STS theory suggests that none of these approaches, in isolation, achieves the joint optimization of social and technical dimensions necessary for high-performing project production systems— motivating the structured comparison in the following section.

## LITERATURE REVIEW AND RESEARCH METHODOLOGY

LITERATURE SELECTION AND REVIEW PROCEDURE

This study is grounded in a structured conceptual review of published literature on EPC project communication, Lean Construction, PPM, AWP, and socio-technical systems theory. Sources were identified through purposive searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracing from foundational works (Koskela, 2000; Hopp & Spearman, 2011; CII, 2015) and industry guidelines from CII, PMI, and PPI. Sources were selected based on relevance to pre-execution planning communication, theoretical or empirical contribution, and citation influence. The review synthesized findings across four thematic areas — EPC planning challenges, Lean collaborative planning, PPM production logic, and AWP deliverable structuring — with STS theory as a cross-cutting analytical lens.

RESEARCH APPROACH AND UNIT OF ANALYSIS

This study employs a qualitative conceptual comparative analysis (Jabareen, 2009) of four communication approaches in EPC pre-execution planning: (1) document-centric conventional practice; (2) Lean Construction; (3) Project Production Management (PPM); and (4) Advanced Work Packaging (AWP). These were selected because they represent distinct paradigms influencing EPC planning practice and collectively span the social, systemic, and procedural dimensions of communication identified in the STS literature. The unit of analysis is pre-

INTERPRETATION OF RESULTS AND KEY FINDINGS

The results indicate that conventional EPC planning communication provides strong governance, documentation control, and contractual traceability, aligning with traditional EPC risk management (PMI, 2021; Merrow, 2011). However, its vertical, document-driven, pushbased logic limits early cross-functional integration and weakens feedback during planning, contributing to late discovery of interface issues, redesign, rework, and schedule disruption (Shen et al., 2017; Love et al., 2018). Critically, conventional systems score low on sociotechnical alignment, addressing the technical-governance dimension while neglecting social and relational conditions necessary for cross-functional trust.

Lean Construction addresses these shortcomings through collaborative planning, shared understanding, and commitment-based coordination (Ballard & Howell, 2003; Koskela, 2000). The relational coordination dimension—frequent, timely, problem-solving communication supported by shared goals and mutual respect (Gittell, 2002)—is a distinctive strength not systematically cultivated by PPM or AWP. However, Lean's reliance on social interaction and informal planning artifacts limits scalability and integration with formal EPC control systems when applied in isolation (O'Connor et al., 2017).

PPM reframes planning communication around production system behavior, linking communication to WIP limits and buffer management for more proactive uncertainty management (Hopp & Spearman, 2011; PPI, 2017). Its relatively low socio-technical alignment

AWP strengthens execution linkage by embedding communication within standardized work packages and explicit readiness criteria (CII, 2015; O’Brien et al., 2013), but its high formalization can reduce flexibility unless supported by collaborative planning behaviors.

COMPLEMENTARITY, SOCIO-TECHNICAL INTEGRATION, AND IMPLICATIONS FOR EPC PRACTICE

No single communication approach sufficiently addresses the full range of pre-execution planning challenges in EPC projects. Viewed through the STS lens, the four approaches occupy distinct but complementary positions: conventional EPC communication provides the governance baseline; Lean addresses the social and behavioral dimension by fostering trust and reliable commitments (Ballard & Howell, 2003; Koskela, 2000); PPM addresses the systemic dimension through quantitative flow and variability management (Hopp & Spearman, 2011); and AWP addresses the procedural dimension by translating plans into execution-ready work packages (CII, 2015).

STS theory suggests this integration constitutes a joint optimization of the social and technical subsystems of EPC planning communication—not merely an additive combination. Lean-based collaborative planning can be embedded within AWP work package development, ensuring readiness criteria are socially negotiated rather than unilaterally imposed, while PPM flow logic informs the sequencing of planning sessions and ensures buffer management is reflected in handoff gate design. PPM's performance metrics and AWP's readiness gates then institutionalize behavioral changes initiated through Lean collaborative planning, creating reinforcing feedback loops between social practice and technical structure. ## CONCLUSIONS

This study compared conventional document-centric EPC planning communication with Lean Construction, PPM, and AWP across eleven criteria grounded in EPC planning, project communication, and socio-technical systems literature. Conventional EPC communication remains document-centric and reactive, offering limited cross-functional integration and trust development. Lean strengthens the social and behavioral dimension through collaborative alignment and commitment-based coordination. PPM provides a technical-systemic foundation through flow and variability management. AWP delivers a procedural link between planning outputs and field execution through structured work packages and readiness criteria.

The key theoretical contribution is a conceptual integrated communication architecture— grounded in STS theory—that positions Lean, PPM, and AWP as complementary across social, systemic, and procedural dimensions, with conventional practices providing the governance baseline. Implementing this architecture requires deliberate cultural change: building crossfunctional trust, shared planning norms, and collaborative commitment cultures. Lean-based planning practices provide the structured collaborative interactions most effective in driving such change, while PPM metrics and AWP readiness gates institutionalize the resulting behavioral shifts (Edmondson, 1999; Schweitzer et al., 2025). This directly aligns with the People, Culture and Change track's focus on cultural transformation and trust development as enablers of improved project production systems.

Future empirical research should test this framework through longitudinal case studies in active EPC projects, examining how Lean collaborative practices affect cultural adoption of AWP readiness criteria, how PPM flow metrics influence cross-functional planning conversations, and under what conditions the integrated architecture most effectively reduces planning variability and improves execution readiness.

## BOUNDARIES AND LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

This study is bounded by its conceptual and analytical nature, drawing on existing literature and industry guidance rather than empirical evidence. The analysis clarifies theoretical and practical distinctions among planning-phase communication approaches and proposes an integration framework for future empirical investigation, rather than measuring quantitative performance impacts. The scope is limited to inter-organizational communication during the pre-execution planning phase of EPC projects; communication in other phases, delivery methods, or alternative frameworks—including digital communication platforms—is outside the scope of this research.

# ABSTRACT

The Parade of Trades game demonstrates how variability that propagates across sequential trades degrades work flow reliability. Prior work pertaining to the use of takt to manage the Parade of Trades explores how planning for handoffs at a fixed beat can accommodate variability. It also shows where waiting occurs and capacity is lost, and how those influence each trade’s time on site and the total project duration. This paper builds on prior work related to the Parade of Trades by adding transfer batching to study how handoff sizing between trades relates to the production system’s performance. The study uses discrete-event simulation. Alternative model variants represent capacity variability and vary in transfer-batch sizes. Results show how transfer-batch sizing affects production system performance. Understanding these results can inform work structuring efforts, for example when developing a takt plan or when sizing capacity buffers and timing handoffs between trades.

## KEYWORDS

Parade of Trades, Takt planning, variability, discrete-event simulation, transfer batch.

## INTRODUCTION

The Parade of Trades game (Tommelein et al., 1999) has become a widely-used learning tool for demonstrating how, due to sequential interdependence of trades, variability propagates and degrades work flow reliability. The game highlights an important insight: even when trades have identical average outputs, variability causes unpredictable handoffs.

Subsequent research has extended the ‘Classic’ Parade of Trades (‘Classic Parade’ here refers to the game formulation presented in Tommelein et al., 1999) by exploring game variations, some of which focused on achieving predictable handoffs. Construction practitioners’ interest in establishing predictable handoffs contributed to the development of the Last Planner® System (Ballard & Tommelein 2021) and, more recently, the increasing adoption of takt planning.

To gain insight into the value of establishing predictable handoffs when designing a production system, the Parade of Trades serves as a reference model and controlled experimental setting in which assumptions about handoff variability can be made explicit, thus enabling comparisons across model variants. In this study, we use discrete-event simulation to compare and contrast production system designs, namely the Classic Parade and two model variants that differ from it in the timing and number of units that get passed from one trade to the next (i.e., the so-called transfer-batch size that defines the handoff).

## LITERATURE

The Classic Parade describes a single-line production system in which sequentially dependent trades pass work through handoffs determined by the roll of a die. The game demonstrates how variability in the quantity of work defined by the outcome of a die roll (contributing to the handoff to the next trade) propagates and affects the downstream trades’ use of their capacity, their actual production rate, and time on site, as well as the inventory between trades and the project duration (Tommelein et al., 1999). The variability in the work that gets done by a trade (called within-task variability by Brodetskaia & Sacks, 2007) or process capability (e.g., Tommelein 2020) is captured by the range and likelihood of the die’s outcomes. The amplification of variability through sequential trades may be viewed from the chaos perspective on construction (e.g., Bertelsen & Koskela, 2003; Fernandez-Solis, 2013), in which outcomes depend on the system’s initial conditions and randomness causes a small deviation from the plan to propagate into large downstream delays. Transfer-batch sizing affects this propagation.

Transfer-batch sizing specifies how much work must be completed before the next trade can start (e.g., one trade must hang some amount of drywall before the follow-on trade can paint it). In flow systems, adherence to a transfer-batch size affects work release timing, inventory between stations, and downstream idle time (Hopp & Spearman, 2008). Smaller transfer batches require more frequent handoffs but enable earlier downstream starts, whereas larger transfer batches reduce handoff frequency at the cost of delayed downstream starts and increased inventory accumulation. With variability, waiting increases as upstream- and downstream work get out of sync, especially when the intention is to keep resource utilization high (Howell et al., 2001; Brodetskaia & Sacks, 2007).

In location-based planning such as takt planning, the definition of zones sets the work package size and therefore functions as a batching decision (Frandson et al., 2015; Tommelein & Emdanat, 2022). Trades may hand off to the next trade an entire zone of work to be completed within the takt, or perhaps a subset of a zone before full zone completion, which in effect reduces the transfer-batch size (Dlouhy et al., 2019). Thus, zone sizing is a work structuring decision with time and cost implications for the project (Tommelein, 2024).

Buffers provide mechanisms to manage variability in handoffs, albeit at a cost in time, inventory, or capacity (Hopp & Spearman, 2008). In construction, buffering takes the form of providing extra capacity, including time allowances in the schedule, or building up inventory between trades (Dlouhy et al., 2019, Poshdar et al., 2018). Inventory buffers in repetitive construction have been sized to protect downstream work from upstream variability (González et al., 2006) or across zones (Horman et al., 2003). The use of capacity buffers is less explored in construction research compared to the use of time- and inventory buffers (Horman, 2001) but it is highly relevant to takted production systems (Frandson et al., 2015).

In the Last Planner® System, workable backlog tasks allow trades to work when their planned task is unavailable; they buffer against capacity loss and time loss (Ballard & Tommelein, 2021). When upstream variability disrupts a handoff in terms of timing or quantity, or when remaining work does not require all of a trade’s available capacity, that capacity goes unexercised unless workable backlog is available, providing tasks the trade can work on instead.

Buffers come in different kinds as the coordination of specialists requires aligning prerequisites at interfaces, including information, materials, and access, that otherwise translate into downstream waiting (Tommelein & Ballard, 1997). The transfer-batch size defines how much work a trade must complete before handing it off to the follow-on trade, and therefore it

determines how much variability accumulates at each handoff and, accordingly, how much buffering the handoff requires. Transfer-batch sizing can therefore be understood as a design choice for managing variability, reflecting Grote’s (2004) distinction between minimizing uncertainty vs. using mechanisms to cope with uncertainty in production system design.

The Parade of Trades game provides a platform to explore production system concepts through simulation. For example, Senior (2011) expands the experimental and measurement features of the Parade by developing an Excel-based Monte Carlo simulation tool, and Han and Park (2011) test reactive managerial actions (e.g., overtime and overmanning) to contrast the firefighting approach with proactive production system design. Tommelein (2020) imposes a planned beat on the Parade logic, and explores the provision of capacity buffers as an upfrontrather than an ad hoc decision to manage variability, thereby linking the game (here referred to as the ‘Takted Parade’) to takt planning.

Discrete-event simulation, e.g., using EZStrobe (Martinez, 2001), enables systematic exploration of production system design alternatives by allowing assumptions to be stated explicitly and held constant across model variants while outcomes are measured. EZStrobe served as a discovery tool to investigate production system design questions in the Takted Parade, providing a controlled experimental setting to explore hypotheses and compare model variants (e.g., Rybkowski et al., 2008). Here, we use EZStrobe to study the sizing of transfer batches as a production system design choice in a system subject to variability. The research question is: How does transfer-batch size affect the Parade of Trades?

## SIMULATION MODEL

MODEL PARAMETERS AND ASSUMPTIONS

This study presents variants of the Takted Parade (Tommelein 2020) by imposing transfer batches of a certain size as the handoff from one trade to the next. It addresses the question how zone count Z affects the losses that become visible when using transfer batches, but it does not include standby (or swing) capacity as a buffer. As in the Classic Parade, the new variants represent five trades (A, B, C, D, E) working in sequence to pass all units of work from start to finish, with the capacity of each trade determined by the outcome of rolling a die.

The model variants are parameterized as follows:

• U is the total number of units to pass (e.g., 100) • Z is the number of transfer batches to pass all units U • L is the lowest die number, and H is the highest die number (e.g., a L/H die may be a

3/7 die. Deterministic models, i.e., models using the all-five die (L = H = 5) without randomness, can provide baseline data for the study.) • E = (L+H)/2 is the expected output per die roll • B = U/Z is the transfer-batch size, and • N =B/E is the expected number of rolls needed to produce the transfer batch Die rolls are independent and identically distributed (IID), meaning that each roll is independent of prior rolls and all trades use the same die.

The transfer-batch size B is a fixed number, chosen by design, that describes how many units a trade must complete before handing off these units to the follow-on trade. Fixed transfer batches require trades to wait until exactly B units are available as input to work on. This waiting will extend the total duration of the Parade. However, transfer batches make handoffs predictable, since each trade knows and can plan for the size of the input they will receive in each handoff. Assuming the handoff is to also occur at a regular time interval, the project can be planned following the beat.

Once a trade has mobilized on site, it may be unable to exercise its capacity for two reasons: (1) the upstream trade has not delivered its handoff that the trade needs as input, or (2) the trade’s capacity exceeds the units needed to complete the transfer batch. In the first case, the downstream trade waits for input; the model tracks this as starving. In the second case, the excess capacity will go unused; the model tracks this excess as lost capacity.

For comparison, note that the Classic Parade enforces no transfer batches (no fixed B), i.e., there is a handoff at the end of each roll. When the trade receives as input fewer units than its capacity , due to upstream variability, it will not be able to exercise all of its capacity. According to the aforementioned definitions of starving and lost capacity, these units are tracked as lost capacity (in contrast, Tommelein et al. 1999 used only the term starving).

TRANSFER BATCH CONFIGURATIONS

This study considers two model variants:

Z = 20 batches (B = 5 units per transfer batch): With E = 5, each transfer batch requires N = B/E = 5/5 = 1 roll on average, creating 20 transfer batches of 5 units each per trade.

Z = 10 batches (B = 10 units per transfer batch): With E = 5, each transfer batch requires N = 10/5 = 2 rolls on average, creating 10 transfer batches of 10 units each per trade.

When transfer batches are passed through the Parade, the structure matches that of a takt plan. In a takt plan, Z would refer to the number of units a trade must complete in one zone, specifically a zone of size B = U/Z units. If every handoff is guaranteed to occur on the takt, the total duration (D) of the deterministic Parade therefore follows the formula D = (S + Z – 1) x T(Z). With E = 5 for all five trades (S = 5) to complete U = 100:

For Z = 20: D = (S + Z – 1) x T(Z) = (5 + 20 – 1) x T(Z) = 24 x T(Z), where T(Z) is the time allotted to one die roll.

For Z = 10: D = (5 + 10 – 1) x T(Z) = 14 x T(Z), where T(Z) now spans the time allotted to two die rolls.

The corresponding two takt plans are illustrated in Figure 1. Of course, variability in die outcomes will cause the actual duration to deviate from these deterministic values. Furthermore, when a transfer batch of a fixed size is imposed, trades likely will starve as well as lose capacity, as is explained next.

HOW STARVING AFFECTS PARADE PERFORMANCE

When transfer-batching is enforced, a Trade Y will starve when its upstream Trade X requires more rolls than the allotted N rolls to complete its transfer batch and consequently causes a time delay in the handoff to Trade Y. For example, if the transfer-batch size is B = 5 units  (N = 1 roll), when Trade X rolls a 3 it will have to roll a second time to reach B, while the follow-on Trade Y waits. Moreover, if B = 10 (N = 2), when Trade X rolls a 3 and then 3 again (total = 6), it will have to roll at least a third- and possibly a fourth time. If that third roll produces 7 units when only 4 more units are needed to complete the batch, Trade X also accumulates 3 units of lost capacity. Thus, requiring a transfer batch results in both Trade Y starving and Trade X having lost capacity. The delay caused by additional rolls propagates downstream and extends the Parade’s total duration.

HOW CAPACITY LOSS AFFECTS PARADE PERFORMANCE

When transfer-batching is enforced, lost capacity occurs when a trade’s die outcome results in more units than the current transfer batch requires. For example, when B = 5 is required (N = 1) and Trade X rolls 3 units, it falls 2 units short of B (insufficient capacity). If Trade X gets a second roll and then rolls 7 units (cumulative = 10 units), it reaches the required B. Accordingly (assuming Trade X was not starving), the transfer batch from Trade X to Trade Y will comprise 5 units and Trade X’s remaining 5 units are tracked as lost capacity. In theory, those 5 units might complete another transfer batch, but the model allows only one handoff at a time. When

COMPUTER MODEL

The model is implemented in EZStrobe (Martinez, 2001) version 4.20 with Microsoft Visio Professional 2024, which calls the Stroboscope Simulation System (Version 7,25,03,27). Figure 2 shows an excerpt of the model structure focused on Trade X representing the active trade and Trade Y the follow-on trade. Each trade in the Parade has an identical structure in the model (combis and queues are replicated with trade-specific names).

The EZStrobe model has four parts: (1) Mobilization and Demobilization of the trade, (2) Production Control enforcing handoffs of the required transfer-batch size, (3) Tracking of starving and lost capacity, and (4) Handoff between trades. Capacity variability [DieOutcome] is introduced by rolling a 3/7 die. Note that the priorities assigned to combis play an important part in the order of execution of combis. Thanks to the parametrization of the model, other values can easily be assigned to any of these (e.g., other probability distributions can be used in lieu of the distribution of a fair L/H die).

At the project start time (the time of model initialization), one unit of Trade X is waiting in queue [StartX]. Trade X arrives on site when combi [MobilizeX] ends, releasing the trade to queue [TradeX]. The timing of this mobilization depends on the trade’s position in the Parade and is planned based on the expected number of rolls needed to receive its first transfer


<!-- Page 6 -->

Proceedings IGLC34, 22-26 June 2026, Singapore 1754

batch (e.g., Trade A mobilizes at time 0, Trade B at N, Trade C at 2N, and so on). Trade X demobilizes when queue [DoneX] accumulates U units. At that time, combi [DemobilizeX] starts and pulls out of its queue [TradeX] so that combi [RollX]will never start again.

*Figure 2: Excerpt of EZStrobe model detailing Trade X*

When the trade is available in [TradeX], the simulation repeatedly loops from rolling the die [RollX] to waiting to roll again [WaitToRollX], then through [NextRollX] back to [TradeX], until the trade demobilizes. The durations of these combis sum to one time unit (e.g., a day, a week, or whatever time unit one roll represents). [RollX] generates an outcome by evaluating the variable [DieOutcome]. This die outcome determines the number of units the trade can produce in that time period, reflecting its capacity, and these units flow to [WorkX]. Whether this capacity can be exercised depends on the availability of units in the prerequisite [InputX] (which may result in starving) and subsequently by the units thus far accumulated in [WorkedX] (which may result in lost capacity). If [InputX] has insufficient input, [WorkX] cannot start and Trade X remains idle (it is starving). [CountStarveX] tracks this and accumulates these units into [StarveX]. Subsequently, any units completed in excess of B are counted as lost capacity, tracked by [CountLostCapX] and accumulated into [LostCapX].

The control mechanism enforces that exactly B units must be completed before releasing work to the follow-on trade. Once [WorkedX] accumulates at least B units, [TransferReadyX]

signals batch completion by checking [CheckX] for the expected number of rolls and releasing B control tokens to [TargetX]. One by one, units then transfer through [TransferBatchX] to [TotalWorkedX], which holds the number of units B required for the transfer batch. Handoff [XY] takes B units from [InputX] and transfers the completed transfer batch to [InputY] for follow-on Trade Y.

This study tracks four metrics, three of which (total duration of the Parade, time on site per trade, and lost capacity) align with those tracked by Tommelein (2020). Total duration is measured as SimTime when all trades have demobilized. For a given Trade X, Time on site per trade is calculated as XEnd - XStart, where XStart is the timestamp when [RollX] first starts and XEnd is when [DemobilizeX] starts. Starving is measured as [StarveX].TotCount. Lost capacity is measured as [LostCapX].TotCount.

Note that, although M02 has a longer deterministic duration than M01, its simulated duration is shorter on average (Figure 3). M01’s simulated duration extends 72% beyond its D, because with a single roll allotted per transfer batch, die-roll variability creates batches that 50% of the time require additional rolls to reach B. Likewise, M02’s simulated duration extends beyond its D as well; however, its extension of 36% is smaller because the two rolls allotted per transfer batch allow for variability pooling. This is one of two reasons why trades spend less time on site in M02 than they do in M01.

TIME ON SITE PER TRADE

In terms of time on site per trade, the Classic Parade’s durations range from 20.5 ± 1.9 (Trade A) to 25.1 ± 1.7 (Trade E), M01’s from 30.0 ± 2.2 to 37.3 ± 1.8, and M02’s from 23.9 ± 2.2 to 30.0 ± 2.5 (Figure 4). In all three model variants, the time on site increases with a trade’s sequential position in the Parade. Standard deviations vary between ±1.6 and ±2.5 across trades, suggesting that variability does not increase downstream even as time on site does.

This pattern reflects the cumulative effect of variability propagating through the Parade. Each subsequent trade inherits the upstream trades’ delays and therefore needs more time on site. Trade A shows the least delay since all input units U are available upon mobilization, and Trade E shows the most delay as it carries delays from all four upstream trades. M02 shows shorter times on site than M01 across all trades despite the delay resulting from the required two rolls per batch. As noted, this is because these two rolls allotted per transfer batch allow for variability pooling, which was not possible with a single roll per batch.

STARVING PER TRADE

In terms of starving, expressed in units per trade, M01 ranges from 0.0 ± 0.0 (Trade A) to 36.3 ± 13.3 (Trade E), and M02 from 0.0 ± 0.0 (Trade A) to 31.8 ± 14.3 (Trade E) (Figure 6). In both model variants, starving increases with the trade's sequential position, by roughly 6 to 13 units per position. The first trade in the Parade (Trade A) does not starve because U units are available from the start, whereas each subsequent trade must wait for its upstream trade to complete and hand off a transfer batch. This delay propagates through the Parade: Trade B experiences delay from Trade A, Trade C from both A and B, and so on, with Trade E inheriting the full accumulated delay. Because M02 has fewer handoffs than M01, M02 trades suffer less from the propagation of starving. This is the second reason why trades spend less time on site in M02 than in M01.

LOST CAPACITY PER TRADE

In terms of lost capacity, also expressed in units per trade, the Classic Parade’s increases from 2.5 ± 2.0 (Trade A) to 25.8 ± 10.9 (Trade E), as explained previously. In contrast, in M01 and M02, lost capacity is relatively uniform across trades: M01’s averages about 50 (range 49.7– 50.0) with standard deviations of ±6.6 to ±6.8, and M02’s averages about 19 (range 18.6–18.9) with standard deviations of ±6.4 to ±6.6 (Figure 5). In transfer-batch model variants, each trade receives a known transfer-batch size B, so lost capacity depends on the die-roll variability that causes time delays to transfer a batch, regardless of the trade’s position in the Parade. Lost capacity in M02 is lower than M01 because of variability pooling.

## DISCUSSION

Comparison of the Classic Parade with M01 and M02 shows a trade-off between the total duration and transfer batch size. The Classic Parade completes faster because trades handoffs occur immediately, but the handoff quantity varies each time. When imposing transfer batches, the handoff quantity is fixed at B, but due to variability in die outcomes additional rolls may be needed to reach the required batch size and the resulting time delays will propagate downstream.

M02 completes faster than M01 in simulation despite having a longer deterministic duration. Two reasons explain this: First, with more rolls per batch, there is opportunity for variability pooling. This reduces the frequency of delayed handoffs. Second, fewer transfer batches mean fewer handoffs at which starving can occur, so less starving propagates downstream, which also leads to less delay to the time on site.

RELEVANCE TO CONSTRUCTION PRACTICE AND TAKT PLANNING

Consider a trade working on 5-unit zones where each zone must be completed before handing it off to the follow-on trade on a set beat (e.g., daily or weekly). Some days the trade completes 3 units (slow day), other days 7 units (fast day). When the trade can complete 7 units but the zone needs only 5, the extra capacity the trade has to produce another 2 is lost capacity (the trade had a fast day but 5 units was enough for the handoff). When the trade completes only 3 and needs a second day to reach 5, the follow-on trade that was scheduled to start on the next beat must wait, i.e., the follow-on trade is starving for work. In the Classic Parade this waiting

does not occur, since whatever is produced gets passed along immediately. However, followon trades then receive unpredictable quantities.

When designing a takt plan, the planner must choose a beat that accounts for this variability. Planners may set the takt below the expected average output, for instance at 3 or 4 units per day rather than 5, as an a priori capacity buffer against starving of the follow-on trade. The unexercised capacity is then lost when production runs faster than planned. Transfer-batch sizing and takt setting therefore carry cost- and schedule implications: starving and lost capacity both incur direct costs, and more frequent handoffs increase coordination effort.

When using a system like the Last Planner®, workable backlog can put unexercised capacity to productive use. Capacity buffers can ensure that every trade meets the takt so that starving does not propagate downstream.

MATHEMATICAL ANALYSIS

Given the configuration of transfer-batch model variants and binary die outcome, the probability of falling short of B in a transfer batch follows a binomial distribution. For M01, the two possible outcomes are rolling 7, which leaves 2 units of lost capacity, or rolling 3, which falls short and needs another roll to reach B = 5. The chance of shortfall is 50%. For M02, the four possible outcomes are 3 then 7, 7 then 3, 7 then 7, and 3 then 3, each with a 25% chance. The first two complete B = 10 exactly. The third leaves 4 units of lost capacity, and the fourth falls short, so the chance of shortfall is now only 25%, half that of M01. When the fourth case occurs, rolling 3-3-7 (12.5% chance) produces 13 units and thus 3 units of lost capacity. Rolling 3-3-3-3 (6.25%) or 3-3-3-7 (6.25%) leave 2 and 6 units of lost capacity respectively.

However, making Z even smaller (using larger transfer batches and fewer handoffs) does not reduce the chance of shortfall, as the binomial analysis reveals. For Z = 5 (N = 4, B = 20), a shortfall occurs when none (all 3’s) or only 1 of the 4 rolls produces a 7, which is possible for 5 sequences out of 16 (31.25% chance, which is lower than M01’s 50% but higher than M02’s 25%). For Z = 2 (N = 10, B = 50), a shortfall occurs when fewer than 5 of the 10 rolls produce 7 (386/1024 possible sequences) (37.70% chance), that is, the chance of shortfall increases even as Z decreases beyond M02’s Z = 10. In summary, increasing N from 1 to 2 decreases the chance of shortfall, but increasing it beyond 2 increases the chance of shortfall, rather than further decreasing it. This non-monotonic behavior suggests that an optimal transfer-batch size exists for a given amount of variability of the die (and thus variability in the expected output).

GENERALIZABILITY

Although the transfer-batch model variants in this study use five trades in a linear sequence, the underlying dynamics apply to larger and more complex Parades as well. The study uses a deliberately simplified model with a binary die to isolate the effect of transfer-batch sizing under controlled conditions and to enable the binomial analysis. Real-world production systems exhibit richer variability profiles, and a trade’s process capability (i.e., the probability distribution of its output) may not be well known a priori, making careful data collection a prerequisite for identifying an appropriate transfer-batch size in practice. Enforcing transfer batches under high variability can amplify the consequences across the Parade. Proper transferbatch sizing is necessary when managing variability in a Parade.

## CONCLUSIONS

This study used discrete-event simulation to explore how transfer batching affects the Parade of Trades. Two transfer-batch model variants were compared to the Classic Parade, tracking total duration as well as time on site, starving, and lost capacity per trade across 1,000 iterations.

The results show that transfer batching makes handoff quantities predictable but is likely to extend the total duration because a trade must complete a transfer batch before handing it off

to the follow-on trade. The binomial analysis reveals that the relationship between transferbatch size and chance of shortfall is not monotonic, suggesting that an appropriate transferbatch size depends on the variability profile and therefore the expected output. Transfer-batch sizing must take into account variability in process capability (as modeled by the die roll). Predictable handoffs in timing and quantity are particularly important in the process of takt planning. The parametrized model presented in this study provides a controlled setting in which such relationships can be explored, both as a learning tool and as a research platform.

Future work could explore the provision of buffers such as capacity- or time buffers as variability management strategies, transfer-batch configurations with different numbers of transfer batches and die probability profiles, and work flows beyond a single trade sequence where completion of a transfer batch may be required as input to one or multiple parades.

Relating performance metrics to costs, allowing work carryover between transfer batches or using workable backlog, and validating findings against planning practice would strengthen the practical applicability of these insights. This study invites practitioners and researchers to reflect on how zoning decisions in (takt) planning affects variability during execution, and to explore other work structuring alternatives that build upon the Parade of Trades.

# DEVELOPING A MISTAKEPROOFING MINDSET TO INCREASE SAFETY CAPACITY

Eugene H. Cheung1, Tim Eigendorf2, Tomisin Kehinde3, Gregory F. Saragih4, & Iris D.

Tommelein5

# ABSTRACT

Safety capacity is the ability to increase the likelihood that work will go right under variableand uncertain conditions. In construction projects, safety has traditionally been managed using lagging indicators, but these offer limited insights to develop safety capacity. Whereas safety management practices can be reactive and compliance-driven, they can also be proactive and anticipation-driven. Specific mistakeproofing (poka yoke) practices can be either one. In this paper, we argue that mistakeproofing practiced with a proactive mindset helps to build safety capacity. We present an approach for developing and sustaining a mistakeproofing mindset by drawing on concepts from uncertainty management (including risk management), Safety-I, Safety-II, and resilience engineering. To demonstrate this mindset, the Work Operation Framework was applied to analyze two construction examples of mistakeproofing related to safety management. Developing this mindset may narrow the gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done. It recognizes that making adaptations is a part of doing work and reflects the intelligence of a (group of) worker(s). The reason for developing a mistakeproofing mindset is to support organizations with continuous improvement to increase their safety capacity.

## KEYWORDS

Mistakeproofing, Poka Yoke, health, safety, Safety-I, Safety-II, safety capacity, mindset, resilience engineering.

## INTRODUCTION

Safety capacity is the ability to increase the likelihood that work will go right under variableand uncertain conditions (Dekker & Tooma 2022). It is a relatively new concept, especially in the construction industry where instead the focus has been on reacting to incidents and figuring out what went wrong. Variable conditions can impact quality, health, and safety, and enhancing these remains a goal in both academic research and industry.

To manage safety under such conditions, organizations rely on performance measurement systems. When things have gone wrong, people collect data from their operations and use lagging performance indicators, such as incident-, injury-, or fatality rates. In contrast, Johnsen (2024) and others argue that both lagging and leading indicators should be integrated to proactively improve safety performance, but they also acknowledge integration challenges. Similarly, OSHA (2019) suggests bridging the gap between reliance on historical data and anticipation of future performance by identifying leading indicators to increase safety capacity.

One way to bridge this gap is to implement lean principles and practices from the Toyota Production System (TPS) and promote a lean mindset (Toyota n.d.), e.g., by using mistakeproofing (poka yoke in Japanese) (Note: For consistency, we spell mistakeproofing as a single word throughout our paper). The premise of this paper is that the practice of mistakeproofing will be enhanced by the cultivation of a mistakeproofing mindset, which in turn will help to increase practitioners’ safety capacity.

The following section presents the literature review related to lean thinking including mistakeproofing, mindsets, risk- and uncertainty management, Safety-I and Safety-II, and resilience engineering. We then describe our research methodology and present a framework for helping people see opportunities to be proactive rather than reactive in managing safety. Using this framework and mistakeproofing examples, we discuss how a mistakeproofing mindset can be developed and sustained. The conclusion section offers directions for future research.

## LITERATURE REVIEW

This literature review starts by introducing terminology. Mistake is defined as “an inadvertent human action that may lead to a defect in a process or product, or harm to a person” (e.g., Tommelein & Demirkesen 2018 p. 18). Although “mistake” and “error” are sometimes used interchangeably, the former is more commonly referred to as a person not doing or not understanding something correctly, whereas the latter more generally refers to a deviation from an expected outcome, whether resulting from a human or machine action. As we focus here on developing a mistakeproofing mindset, which pertains to human behavior, we use the term “mistake” consistently throughout the paper to denote both.

Mistakeproofing is defined as using a device or practice to either prevent or detect abnormalities that might be detrimental either to product or process quality or to a person’s health and safety (after Saurin et al. 2012). Its application in quality- and safety management is quite broad, although the expertise in these areas may reside in different people (Stewart & Grout 2001).

One way to practice mistakeproofing is using the Work Operation Framework, formalized in the construction context by Tommelein and Demirkesen (2018). This Framework includes four principles upstream of a mistake to “make the occurrence of a mistake less likely” (namely eliminate, prevent, replace, and facilitate) and two principles downstream of a mistake to “alleviate the impact after the mistake occurred” (detect and mitigate) (Tommelein 2019). Figure 1 shows a simplified version.

The Framework can be used to describe concerns and countermeasures. A “concern describes something that might go wrong,” and a “countermeasure describes a mistakeproofing practice either to reduce the likelihood of the mistake being made or to alleviate the impact of the mistake after it has been made (Tommelein 2024).” When a concern is identified, one or several countermeasures may be proposed to address it. The identification of concerns and countermeasures is iterative and aligns with the PDCA cycle for continuous improvement, concepts well known in lean management.

Lagging indicators refer to historical events (alleviate impact after occurrence), e.g., they may quantify a fatality rate. In contrast, leading indicators refer to proactive measures (making occurrence less likely), e.g., they may quantify the effectiveness of an organization’s safety performance (Toellner 2001, OSHA 2019). The ability to anticipate and address concerns serves as a leading indicator of safety capacity.*

This ability may be nurtured by developing a mistakeproofing mindset. Dweck (2006) defines a mindset as a set of beliefs that guides how a person interacts with the world. A fixed mindset is the belief that skills and knowledge come naturally to a person with little motivation to challenge the current way of thinking. In contrast, a growth mindset is the belief that skills and knowledge are not fixed, but traits that can be acquired or improved through effort over time. In the context of mistakeproofing, a growth mindset is essential because it encourages the questioning of existing practices and actively seeks opportunities for continuous improvement.

The ability to anticipate concerns aligns with a risk management mindset, at least to some degree. Pym (1987) defines a risk management mindset as “identifying, analyzing, and responding to risk factors throughout the life of a project and in the best interests of its objectives.” Whereas project risk management may consider both threats and opportunities, it is all-too-commonly operationalized through the adoption of a downside view of uncertainty (i.e., identifying what might go wrong and taking for granted what is going right). In general, uncertainty refers to the “lack of certainty” that may lead to positive or negative outcomes, but in practice, risk management tends to focus more on threats, adverse events, and their mitigation (Ward & Chapman 2003). Even when the aim is to improve performance and create opportunities, the analytical starting point is typically potential failure rather than existing successful performance.

Advocating for a more balanced mindset, Grote (2003) distinguishes two approaches to uncertainty management. One approach seeks to minimize uncertainty through central planning, continuous monitoring, and minimizing degrees of freedom at the point of execution. The other emphasizes coping with uncertainty when conditions are variable. The first approach may be appropriate in predictable environments, whereas the second becomes increasingly important in more complex settings. As an uncertainty management approach, mistakeproofing may help to reduce sources of uncertainty from the system, however, it does not eliminate the need for adaptability when uncertainty cannot be designed out.

To distinguish mindsets for understanding safety management, Hollnagel et al. (2013) talk about Safety-I and Safety-II. Safety-I defines safety in terms of adverse outcomes and tends to include blaming people after-the-fact for what went wrong. It follows a “find and fix” approach, looking for failures and tracing back their causes, and then eliminating these causes to prevent reoccurrence. Safety-I simply assumes things will go right when preventing them from going wrong, without any motivation to examine what was done correctly. This type of mindset stems from outcome and hindsight biases, known as shortcut thinking (Scanlon & Jacobson 2025). Outcome bias is the judgment of the quality of a decision made based on the result of an event. Hindsight bias is the belief that the outcome of an event would have been predicted before it occurred, even if the information was not available beforehand (Hollnagel et al. 2015). Acknowledging both cognitive biases, Hollnagel et al. (2015) suggest that Safety-I is a causality credo, based on the “belief that adverse outcomes happen because something goes wrong.”

In contrast, Safety-II focuses on increasing the likelihood that tasks will be performed correctly in order to improve safety performance. It includes the study of what usually goes right. Contrary to Safety-I, this mindset assumes that a system’s performance involves many interrelated components and multiple variations. For mistakeproofing, this implies that preventing mistakes requires not only eliminating potential failures but also understanding how successful adaptations emerge during the normal execution of operations. In this sense, conventional risk-management aligns with Safety-I, whereas mistakeproofing builds on the foundation and extends it through Safety-II.

A gap exists between work-as-imagined (theoretical) and work-as-done (reality) (e.g., Shorrock 2016). Work-as-imagined refers to the idealized work procedures designed by management based on assumptions and predictions. Work-as-done reflects the reality of work performance with adaptations. A mistakeproofing mindset needs to acknowledge the reality of work-as-done rather than rely solely on the fantasy of work-as-imagined. It involves designing systems that tolerate human variability and celebrate human creativity, that lead to emergent adaptations and facilitate recovery when variability manifests itself.

Recognizing the value of emergent adaptations on the performance of complex systems, Hollnagel (2012) defines resilience engineering as a system having the four abilities to “adjust its functioning prior to, during, or following changes and disturbances, so that it can sustain required operations under both expected and unexpected conditions.” These four abilities refer to “sustain,” “respond,” “monitor,” and “learn.” Resilience engineering requires a mindset that involves learning proactively how things usually go well and developing methods to enhance a system’s capabilities. This focus on adaptation aligns with Safety-II thinking.

However, in practice, safety management may emphasize regulatory compliance, treating work variations as mistakes rather than potential improvements. When safety management focuses solely on compliance with work-as-imagined, it creates a “brittle” system in which the gap between procedure and reality widens, increasing the risk of unpredicted failure (Woods 2015).

The development of a resilient mindset – including a mistakeproofing mindset – that proactively monitors the gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done is a leading indicator of safety capacity. It identifies where workers are forced to adapt or violate procedures to get the job done. By treating these adaptations not as violations but as signals of system design flaws, organizations can implement “upstream” mistakeproofing measures before an incident occurs. As Hollnagel (2018) suggests, the ability to anticipate and monitor these operational gaps is the hallmark of a safe system. Consequently, fostering a mindset that embraces the complexities of work-as-done is the ultimate form of cognitive mistakeproofing, transforming the workforce from a source of mistakes into a source of system resilience.

## METHODOLOGY

We propose and formulate an approach for developing and sustaining a mistakeproofing mindset and apply it to construction safety management, aiming to help people develop safety capacity. To do so, we leverage principles and methods from lean construction, safety management paradigms including Safety-I and Safety-II, and resilience engineering. This formulation is to support the transition from a compliance-based to a lean philosophy-based safety education approach.

To illustrate what drives a mistakeproofing mindset, we present the Work Operation Framework and use it to analyze two construction examples. These examples were selected because they address common safety concerns in construction. The purpose is to show how the mindset can be applied to narrow the gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done. The methodology follows the PDCA cycle to illustrate that practicing mistakeproofing is iterative. Each example was analyzed through multiple iterations to show that implementing

## MISTAKEPROOFING MINDSET

To position a mistakeproofing mindset as a means to increase safety capacity, a distinction must be made between observable practices and the mindset that precedes and governs them. Drawing on Dweck’s (2006) concept of a fixed versus a growth mindset, a mistakeproofing mindset can be a leading indicator for safety capacity. In practice, a person with this mindset does not just follow a safety rule but actively seeks ways to make the mistake impossible even in novel situations where a specific “rule” or “practice” has not yet been established (Grout 2007).

A mindset is dynamic and must be developed and sustained. To develop a mistakeproofing mindset, a person needs to recognize their current way of thinking. However, because a person’s mindset largely operates outside of conscious awareness, this self-recognition may be obstructed by biases to be overcome. Therefore, the development of the mindset must be structured methodologically. From an educational perspective, as suggested in Bloom’s Taxonomy, a person’s capability to mistakeproof may be built sequentially. Bloom’s Taxonomy is “designed to be a classification of the student behaviors which represent the intended outcomes of the educational process” that is “organized from simple to complex [...] behavior” (Bloom et al. 1956). Applying this logic, one cannot expect a person to outright be able to create new countermeasures, given that ‘create’ reflects the highest level of Bloom’s Taxonomy. A person’s ability to create something new will be aided by first understanding, e.g., the principles presented in the Work Operation Framework.

The development of a mistakeproofing mindset focuses on shifting from a compliancebased to a lean philosophy-based safety education. Traditional safety education provides a baseline of knowledge, whereas education for a mistakeproofing mindset goes deeper by introducing principles from TPS. Specifically, once the principles are taught, hands-on training may be provided to help the person practice. Training may make use of the Work Operation Framework to analyze mistakeproofing examples, where participants learn to question current state concerns before they become mistakes. In addition, to bridge the gap between work-asimagined and work-as-done, pedagogical simulations such as the “Mistakeproofing! It’s in the Cards” game by Tommelein (2024) allow a person to practice lean thinking in a risk-free environment.

Sustainability is achieved when, through continuous practice, mistakeproofing becomes a habit. It is the continuous improvement mindset itself that contributes to ensuring that things go right, and this builds safety capacity. Importantly, sustaining a mistakeproofing mindset also requires preserving a sense of situational awareness. When a countermeasure becomes part of the ‘normal’ environment, the original concern and rationale for it may no longer be obvious: mistakeproofing applications must be documented. In practice, one countermeasure can introduce many new concerns to be addressed. If not duly documented, a concern may be addressed by a countermeasure, but the implementation of that countermeasure itself may already have been the source of concerns. The progression is not linear but manifold. The following two examples illustrate progressions of concerns and countermeasures.

EXAMPLE 1: MOBILE ELEVATED WORK PLATFORMS (MEWPS)

Falls are the leading cause of death in construction, with 370 fatal falls recorded in 2024 out of 1,032 total construction fatalities (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2026). Fall protection ranked as OSHA’s most frequently cited violation in fiscal year 2024 (OSHA 2025). A mistakeproofing mindset can help to address safety concerns related to falls when working at height.

When constructing a structural-steel building, field-welded connections will require working at height. In this context, equipment such as mobile elevated work platforms (MEWPs) can play a critical role in reducing the likelihood of falls.

*Figure 2: Bolted steel moment resisting frame (Source: ConXtech (n.d.) visited 11 February*

2017) Concern: Completing a field-welded beam-to-column connection requires workers working at height to wear a harness and tie themselves off as they position themselves to weld around the joint. This work exposes them for an extended period of time to fall hazards. Countermeasure: A steel moment-resisting frame with welded connections is replaced by bolted connections. A ‘shoe’ is shop-welded onto the column. On site, steel beams slide into it (Figure 2) to form a secure connection, and are then bolted in place. This work can be done by a worker standing on a MEWP and in a shorter amount of time, and is therefore safer.

*Figure 3: MEWP (Source: WSM Training (n.d.) visited 29 January 2026)*

Concern: Workers need to perform tasks at height. Accessing high or hard-to-reach areas using traditional tools like ladders or scaffolding can be challenging and risky. When climbing, workers risk losing balance and falling from height. Countermeasure: A MEWP provides a safer way for workers to reach elevated work areas (Figure 3). It reduces the risk of falling and allows workers to work more conveniently at height. Workers can perform tasks in an optimal work posture, reducing bending and stretching.

Concern: MEWPs are controlled manually and based on sight by authorized operators. Despite OSHA requiring all MEWP operators to receive training, mistakes may occur during MEWP operation. An operator may raise the MEWP too high and collide with an overhead obstruction. Countermeasure: A wireless overhead protection sensor device can be installed on MEWPs (Figure 4). This exposure increases the risk of injury or longer-term health issues. Countermeasure: Anti-fatigue mats on MEWPs reduce stress on workers’ feet and legs (Figure 5). Their cushioning provides comfort during long working hours. Although no specific regulation prohibits the placement of anti-fatigue mats on MEWPs, users must follow safety requirements when installing them (Plessis 2025).*

EXAMPLE 2: SAFETY SHOES

Foot injuries represent a significant and preventable workplace risk. OSHA’s mandate of protective footwear under standard 29 CFR 1910.136 requires employers to ensure employees wear safety shoes in areas where there is danger of foot injuries due to falling or rolling objects, or electrical hazards (OSHA n.d.-b).

This example illustrates how personal protective equipment addresses impact-related risks while simultaneously introducing secondary concerns related to ergonomics and, in sensorenabled applications, data privacy. It highlights how mistakeproofing extends beyond initial protection toward ongoing risk awareness.

## DISCUSSION

The contribution of this study is to position the mistakeproofing mindset as a leading indicator of improved safety performance and safety capacity. The notion of safety capacity is relatively new, and it must be understood as the ability to ensure that work goes right even under variable conditions. In this context, it is vital to distinguish between capacity, which is what you are capable of and can do, and performance, which is what you actually do. For example, a site may have safe lifting equipment and trained workers but still experience accidents when time pressure leads people to skip procedures. Consequently, the absence of mistakes does not necessarily equal the presence of safety. Therefore, developing a mistakeproofing mindset

Developing a mistakeproofing mindset to increase safety capacity

Proceedings IGLC34, 22-26 June 2026, Singapore 386

requires a person to question the extent to which something goes right to overcome biases and adopt Safety-II thinking.

A mistakeproofing mindset contrasts with the Safety-I mindset and its causality credo. Any countermeasure addressing a concern should be viewed as temporary rather than permanent. New concerns will arise from a current countermeasure. This reinforces the need for continuous improvement and requiring mistakeproofing to be practiced iteratively in line with the Kaizen philosophy. In this way, the mistakeproofing mindset encourages questioning “what goes right” rather than just “what goes wrong” in risk management. The safety shoe example illustrates this: whereas traditional steel-toe boots address impact risks, they also introduce concerns such as ergonomic fatigue. Thus, in practice, the leading indicator is neither the wearing of the boot nor the use of the sensor, but the ability to recognize that the current state countermeasure is likely the source of a future-state concern.

Variations are central to understanding the development of a mistakeproofing mindset. This is because variations reflect workers’ ability to adapt to circumstances in their work. Even though Hollnagel (2012) suggests differentiating between work-as-imagined and work-as-done in managing safety, this paper proposes that developing a mistakeproofing mindset helps reduce the brittleness described by Woods (2015) by making gaps visible. In this sense, narrowing the gap reflects the presence of a mistakeproofing mindset.

A person’s adaptations should be viewed as an expression of intelligence rather than a violation of a standard, as suggested in resilience engineering. For example, when a person intuitively modifies a workspace, they are practicing mistakeproofing. One such example is adding an anti-fatigue mat to a MEWP. At the organizational level, if people capture concerns that drive adaptation, they gain access to leading indicators. This access to operational insight encourages organizations to investigate how work goes right during normal operations, overcoming hindsight bias and outcome bias. Consequently, the ability to recognize work variations with this mindset entails anticipating both expected and unexpected outcomes, which gradually strengthen organizational resilience.

Once a mistakeproofing mindset is present, sustaining it can improve safety capacity. Rather than focusing on the number of iterations, the quality of learning across iterations reflects an organization’s safety capacity. For this learning to occur, organizational support is required to educate, train, and encourage people to practice using, for example, the Work Operation Framework in real-life situations. Through such support, frequent practice helps a person to turn the mistakeproofing mindset into a habit. Over time, the person can influence others to adopt the same mindset and achieve continuous improvement collectively. Arguably, the mindset is not limited to safety and health concerns but also includes design and quality.

## CONCLUSIONS

This paper positioned mistakeproofing not only as the practice of identifying concerns and addressing them by countermeasures, but as a mindset. We hypothesized that mistakeproofing and a mistakeproofing mindset can serve as leading indicators of improved safety performance and safety capacity. In this context, the notion of safety capacity is relatively new, and it must be understood as the ability to ensure that work goes right even under variable conditions. It is presumed that improving safety capacity suggests that safety performance may improve over time. This focus on the development of safety capacity moves safety management beyond compliance and towards continuous improvement.

Furthermore, this paper demonstrated that mistakeproofing is not a linear process but an iterative process drawing on the PDCA cycle of continuous improvement. The leading indicator is the ability to recognize these cycles of improvement. This ability represents a state of mindfulness, of constant alertness, in which current countermeasures introduce multiple future state concerns.
